title: Persistence
summary: Persistence is the tactic that covers everything an adversary does to keep access across reboots, credential resets, and partial remediation, and it is the reason incidents that appear contained often resume weeks later. Behaviours in this tactic include modifying registry run keys and startup folders, installing services or daemons, creating scheduled tasks and cron entries, adding accounts or SSH authorised keys, abusing external remote services such as VPN or remote desktop gateways, planting web shells in application directories, and hijacking legitimate authentication pathways so that a token or certificate continues to work after the original password is changed. Defenders have good theoretical telemetry here because persistence usually requires a write to a durable location, and those writes are visible in registry auditing, file integrity monitoring, service and task creation events, directory service change logs, and cloud identity audit records. The practical difficulty is a very high legitimate baseline. Software deployment, agent updates, and administrators constantly create the same artifacts, so each event in isolation is weak. Compounding this, sophisticated adversaries prefer persistence that is indistinguishable from normal platform behaviour, such as a new OAuth application consent or a certificate added to an enterprise application, which may leave no endpoint trace at all. Detection therefore depends on inventories, change control correlation, and reviewing every new durable artifact against a known-good baseline, ideally with the identity and process that created it.
objectives: Enumerate the main persistence locations and mechanisms across endpoints, directories, cloud identities, and network services.
Explain which logging and auditing configurations are prerequisites for detecting persistence, and what gaps remain without them.
Correlate a newly created durable artifact with the identity and process responsible for creating it.
Use change management and asset inventory data to suppress expected persistence-like activity without losing genuine anomalies.
Recognise identity-layer persistence such as application consent, federated trust changes, and long-lived credentials.
Produce a remediation checklist that removes persistence rather than only the visible malware.
